home.title: Find what's changing on Earth, where, and if it's real.
home.subtitle: Six variables measured by NASA satellites and models.
home.earthAlt: Illustration of Earth seen from space

precipitation.name: Precipitation
precipitation.def: Total amount of rain and snow that reaches the ground, in millimetres per day.

solar_radiation.name: Solar radiation
solar_radiation.def: Sunlight that reaches the surface under real sky conditions, in kWh per square metre per day.
solar_radiation.alt: Sun with rays over the horizon

soil_moisture.name: Soil moisture
soil_moisture.def: How wet the top layer of soil is, as a fraction from 0 (dry) to 1 (saturated).

surface_runoff.name: Surface runoff
surface_runoff.def: Water that flows over the land surface instead of soaking in, in millimetres per day.
surface_runoff.alt: Stream of water flowing over land

no2.name: Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)
no2.def: A polluting gas from traffic, industry and fires, measured as a column of air above us.

ozone.name: Total ozone (O₃)
ozone.def: The ozone in the full column of air. It shields life from harmful ultraviolet light.

state.sumRising: {{name}} is rising by {{rate}} per decade. This is unlikely to be chance.
state.sumFalling: {{name}} is falling by {{rate}} per decade. This is unlikely to be chance.
state.sumNone: We can't tell a real change from natural variation (p = {{p}}). Try a longer period.
state.sumInsufficient: There isn't enough data to test a trend.
state.needMore: Widen the period to at least 10 years or pick a region with more data.

glossary.p: How likely a trend this strong is by pure chance. Below 0.05 is called significant.
glossary.sen: The median rate of change across all pairs of points. It resists outliers.
glossary.anomaly: A value minus the typical value for that calendar month.
glossary.ci: The range where the true rate of change probably lies, with 95% confidence.

states.errorNetwork: The server is not reachable. It may be waking up.

method.title: How we test for trends
method.intro: Every claim in this app comes from a simple, repeatable recipe. Here it is in plain language.
method.s1: We subtract the typical value of each calendar month. What is left is called an anomaly, so summer rain does not look like a trend.
method.s2: This test asks if values tend to go up or down over time without assuming a straight line. It gives a p-value.
method.s3: The median of all pairwise slopes. It gives the rate of change per decade and is hard to fool with outliers.
method.s4: A second opinion. We fit a straight line, test its slope with a t-test and show a 95% confidence interval. If both methods agree we say so.
method.s5: On a map we test hundreds of cells, so some would look significant by luck. The Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction fixes that.
method.s6: If p is 0.05 or higher we write 'no clear trend', never 'no change'. Absence of proof is not proof of absence. We also refuse to test periods under 10 years or with over 30% of data missing.
method.val: The team compares slope and p-value for sample series against NASA Giovanni and KNMI Climate Explorer. Results are listed in the repository.
method.src: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and CERES), NASA GLDAS and OMI via Earthdata and Giovanni. Variables marked 'Demo data' are synthetic until their ingestion runs.
